While deep learning-based end-to-end neural image symbol recognition (NISR) achieves high accuracy for common words, it often generates nonsensical predictions for unseen terms like candidates' names and ballot instructions. We introduce a stochastic hydrodynamic formulation for interacting Bose gases, derived from the Beliaev equation of motion for two-component massive Boson fields. This approach, termed the Phase-space Random Quantum Hydrodynamics (spRQHD), functions as a non-perturbative, classical, stochastic theory. It serves as a hydrodynamic counterpart to the Beliaev approximation, offering a systematic expansion that incorporates thermal and quantum fluctuations beyond hydrodynamic gradients. When applied to uniform gases, spRQHD reproduces a known perturbative Bogoliubov spectrum; for gases with finite interactions, it generates a set of closed-loop integral equations describing quantum stochastic fluid dynamics. These equations define a hierarchy of constitutive relations, which, when truncated, yield a practical, closed hydrodynamic model suitable for simulations. We demonstrate the utility of this framework by deriving a two-fluid model and validating it against the Beliaev solution for evaporating gases. Furthermore, we report on the direct integration of the underlying stochastic hydrodynamic equations via a spectral method. This numerical technique allows for the computation of quantum correlations in initial conditions and their evolution over time, providing a powerful tool for investigating quantum correlations in Bose gases using a non-perturbative, classical, stochastic approach.

Human learning frequently occurs within a teacher-student framework, where an instructor guides a pupil through demonstrations, queries, and feedback to facilitate knowledge construction. Conversely, automated systems can adopt this same dynamic to acquire new domains of knowledge through an instructor-pupil framework. This framework comprises three primary phases: the demonstration phase, the questioning phase, and the feedback phase. While significant progress has been achieved in both academic research and real-world applications of knowledge acquisition (QA), systematic investigations remain necessary to identify existing gaps and potential future directions. This survey outlines the instructor-pupil framework, detailing its three stages and associated methodologies. It further categorizes recent approaches and identifies open challenges, with a specific focus on feedback mechanisms, semantic graph construction, knowledge representation, and evaluation strategies to streamline the process. Ultimately, we propose a unified, end-to-end framework designed to make the knowledge acquisition procedure more efficient and effective.

This framework will be open-source, enabling the automatic comparison of multiple systems across a structured schema: first by decomposing target domains into a semantic structure (comprising a question, context, knowledge-triple, and fact-triple), and second by generating a knowledge-triple for a given query and context utilizing an active learning strategy. We will also examine the three phases of the instructor-pupil knowledge acquisition process, proposing specific solutions for each. Furthermore, we will introduce an automated evaluation method to assess the effectiveness of the feedback function, as well as the underlying knowledge structure and related triples. Finally, we will outline a potential four-phase pipeline for an instructor-pupil system: (i) domain-specific vocabulary collection, (ii) construction of an initial semantic structure (graph), (iii) refinement of the graph via a feedback mechanism, and (iv) acquisition of structured knowledge through fact-triple generation. We will conclude by addressing real-world applications and outlining future research directions. The proposed instructor-pupil framework will be accompanied by an accompanying open-source repository.

Expectation maximization is a widely adopted technique for addressing various maximum likelihood problems within graphical models. To enable a straightforward implementation of this approach without relying on approximate methods, we introduce a simple, uncomplicated algorithm for calculating the maximum likelihood (or maximum probability in the case of Markov random fields) at each iteration. This addition creates a fully practical solution, potentially making it feasible in previously difficult scenarios. Consequently, this new method could serve as a viable alternative to other techniques, such as variational methods, for solving maximum likelihood tasks in graphical models. Furthermore, beyond the iterative expectation maximization framework, the algorithm itself holds independent value; it establishes the first direct, exact, and polynomial-time method for performing "maximum" inference in first-order logic-based neuro-symboleistic reasoning systems. We provide the details of this algorithm, termed simple peeling, alongside corresponding C++ code available at https://github.com/AmirAhliter/SimplePeeling. Although the algorithm is exact and operates on a linear-like time complexity, its runtime in specific contexts may still be influenced by the complexity of the underlying maximum problem; in such instances, the complexity of the graphical model's structure will be discussed. We also briefly compare this method with other existing approaches. Finally, we present a limited exploration of potential applications for this algorithm in neuro-symboleistic reasoning systems and other areas.

Soccer managers and coaches frequently face significant decisions during games that can alter the game's trajectory and ultimate result. While players on the field must also adapt their actions in real-time to secure victory, neither group possesses explicit knowledge of the optimal strategies for specific match states. This study introduces a novel state-space reduction technique combined with an actor-critic algorithm based on distributional dynamic programming to derive a principled policy suitable for soccer. Additionally, the derived policy offers actionable guidance for managers, coaches, and even players regarding in-game decisions. Validation using real-world data from the German Bundesliga confirms the practical value of this methodology for both professional teams and individual players. Ultimately, this work provides a first-principles-based decision-making framework applicable to soccer and potentially other sports, as well as other domains involving strategic decision-making. This study demonstrates the remote operation of a single optical setup to generate two-dimensional Laser Doppler Vibrometer (LDV) velocity maps across a test surface. By employing a "single-point" LDV configuration, we tracked the Doppler frequency shifts produced by linearly polarized light at varying locations. These shifts were converted into 2X and 2Y velocity components using a digital hologram, which enabled the determination of the LDV sensing vector's orientation relative to the surface at each point. Consequently, a feedback loop was established to adjust the vector's direction (via X and Y rotation angles) at every location so that it aligns perpendicularly with the surface. Once alignment was achieved, the 2X and 2Y velocities were derived from the Doppler frequency, allowing for the creation of full 2D LDV velocity maps. The effectiveness of this approach was validated on both flat and curved surfaces, as well as on vibrating surfaces. To the best of our knowledge, this method represents the first implementation of a "single-point" LDV system capable of generating 2D velocity maps through distant, remote control. Such a system holds significant potential for applications where providing a second LDV head is logistically challenging. We examine the linear and nonlinear spectral stability, as well as the stability and existence of solitary waves, for the equation of an anharmonic oscillator coupled to a wave equation (or an anharmonic solitary wave interacting with a wave packet). This system arises as a special case of the Klein--Gordon equation paired with an anharmonic potential, serving as a model for an interface between media with distinct physical properties. Leveraging a variational approach, we establish the existence of anharmonic solitary waves and demonstrate that nonlinear stability follows if the initial condition is a perturbation of such a wave. Conversely, we prove that instabilities—whether due to boundary layer formation, linear dispersion relations with imaginary frequencies, or nonlinear resonance between the anharmonic solitary wave and a packet of linear waves—inevitably result in nonlinear instability. These findings confirm that linear and nonlinear stabilities are intrinsically linked, with the anharmonicity of the potential well acting as the source of instability when the spectrum exhibits imaginary frequencies. Numerical simulations of an initial Gaussian pulse corroborate these results. Additionally, we derive a precise characterization of eigenfunctions corresponding to discrete eigenvalues, a description that may prove useful in broader applications. The study of this system provides insights applicable to other scenarios involving the coupling of anharmonic and harmonic (or nearly harmonic) oscillators, including the context of solitary waves in $\ube$-Gaussian nonlocal nonlinear Schr$\backslash$e -matter fields.

At colliders, long-lived particles manifest as displaced vertices outside the main calorimeter or as missing energy. At Belle II, D meson decays producing photons with energies of 2.5 GeV or less are indistinguishable from neutrino missing energy. We evaluate the sensitivity of Belle II to the visible decay spectrum of axion-like particles (ALPs) at the 2.5--6 GeV range using simulated data, and we recalculate the sensitivity to its missing decay spectrum. We demonstrate that combining both decay spectra significantly enhances Belle II's ability to detect ALPs generated in B meson decays, particularly at resonant masses where the visible spectrum offers superior sensitivity. Furthermore, we establish that future experiments like FASER2 and SHiP could exploit displaced vertices in B meson decays to identify ALPs, potentially extending the reach of such searches by orders of magnitude at specific masses. These interdependent sensitivities among current and upcoming experiments could effectively explore the parameter space for minimal seesaw-type alien axions and for majoron models derived from the seesaw mechanism. Additionally, we discuss the potential for Belle II to identify non-resonant dark photon-like particles through oscillations in the missing energy spectrum arising in B meson decays.

This study evaluates embedding-based methods for identifying post-contextualized language failures during few-shot semantic alteration detection tasks. The research examines state-of-the-art techniques used by Babel, XLNet, RoBERTa, and contextualized models with attention mechanisms, which are capable of processing modified texts to determine if they represent alterations of the original. Experimental results indicate that models processing both modified and unmodified versions of sentences perform poorly, often failing to distinguish between them. Surprisingly, even pre-trained models designed for natural inference tasks, such as XLNet and BERT (via the Sentence Pair approach), struggle when given pairs of original and modified texts, sometimes treating them as entailment problems. These findings suggest that current state-of-the-art models are ill-suited for this specific task and require further fine-tuning. Additionally, the work introduces a simple baseline method that leverages lexical overlap between original and modified texts, which outperforms all embedding-based approaches. Ultimately, the study concludes by proposing effective strategies to enhance the performance of existing models on this challenge. The dataset utilized is available at: https://github.com/linguistics-ucsd/ChangeDetection. Code for this project can be accessed at: https://github.com/Anushree-1999/Contextualized_Language_Frameworks_for_Semantic_Alteration_Detection:_Insights_Learned.

We propose reexamining the spin measurements of 11 binary black holes and one black hole–neutron star system, largely derived from the line broadening of Fe K$\alpha$ fluorescence. These observations provide an upper limit on the product of a black hole's mass and its spin. By combining this constraint with the lower limit imposed by the absence of superradiance growth for each specific mass, we can estimate the upper bound of the axion mass for various dark matter candidates. This method yields tighter constraints than previously used approaches, potentially shifting the favored ultralight dark matter model from the "axion" to the "axon." Furthermore, this technique relies solely on the upper limit of the black hole spin and does not require precise spin determination; consequently, it remains applicable even when future measurements only refine the current upper limits. This study was not driven by the expectation that the resulting axion mass upper limit would surpass the most direct constraint of $\sim10^{-19}$ eV, which stems from the binary pulsar limit on long-range axion-dyon dipole interactions. Rather, our goal is to explore whether the spin of a black hole influences its gravitational wave emission. If the axion mass lower limit is eventually elevated beyond $10^{-19}$ eV, the combination of our method and existing limits could impose a significant restriction on the validity of the standard axion potential. Additionally, this analysis does not depend on the no-hair theorem, as it requires only the superradiance growth condition and the fact that a black hole's spin cannot exceed unity.

We present a Monte Carlo method for simulating the quantum dynamics of a harmonic oscillator under non-Gaussian acceleration, such as under the influence of a delta-function force. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on discretizing time for numerical integration, our technique discretizes the spatial coordinate to evaluate the influence functional via a Metropolis algorithm applied to a discretized path integral. It remains uncertain whether feedback mechanisms linked to supernovae (SN) or black hole (BH) activity regulate star formation at the high mass end. We examined the roles of bulge properties and central surface brightness in this context using a sample of 20,000 galaxies with masses ranging from $10^{9}$ to $10^{11} M_{\odot}$. The data indicates that both larger bulges and higher central surface brightness contribute to a star formation rate (SFR) decline as galaxy mass increases beyond $2 \times 10^{10} M_{\odot}$. Furthermore, the influence of the B/T ratio on the turn-over mass is more significant than that of the actual bulge mass. Our findings suggest that the Kroupa initial mass function (IMF) is unlikely responsible for the turn-over, as the required change in the IMF slope at low masses contradicts established constraints. Instead, we propose that the turn-over results from a shift in gas distribution: at lower masses, star formation is driven by disks, whereas at higher masses, bulges dominate and exhibit lower specific star formation rates due to rapid gas depletion. This aligns with observations that B/T correlates more strongly with specific SFR than with total mass. To replicate the slope of the turn-over, the bulge must be approximately ten times more efficient at depleting its gas supply than the disk. We conclude that feedback mechanisms, if they are involved, must be more potent in bulges than in disks at these elevated masses. Additionally, we discuss how these results relate to the turnover seen in the "M*-BH mass" correlation and the turnover in the central FUV flux–mass relation reported by Behroozi et al. (2013). Finally, we address the implications of our results for the "inside-out" galaxy formation model. Potential contradictions arising from the correlation between black hole mass and bulge mass are also considered. These conclusions were derived assuming a Salpeter IMF; we clarify the adjustments necessary if a Chabrier IMF is adopted rather than a Kroupa IMF. Ultimately, the relative contributions of the bulge and disk to star formation at the high mass end depend on the assumed IMF shape, whereas the overall trends remain consistent across different IMF choices. We report the detection of atmospheric rotation in the ultra-cool dwarf 2MASS0431−7325 (Te = 1300 ± 50 C), whose spin-up from a quiescent state is evident in its light curve. This event is analogous to the cataclysmic variable SW Sextantis but represents the first such occurrence outside that system's class. Utilizing 11 years of Kepler photometry and radial velocity data, we determined a mass of 0.053 ± 0.004 M_sun and a radius of 0.117 ± 0.005 R_sun, placing the white dwarf donor on the Born-again Luminous AGB (LAGN) track. We find that simple planetary impact models fail to explain the observed line-profile changes, whereas a tidally stripped planet successfully accounts for both the light curve variations and profile evolution. Furthermore, we identify contradictions between this model and recent formation scenarios, proposing instead that the planet originated as a brown dwarf captured from interstellar space. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for brown dwarf formation channels and catastrophic events involving brown dwarfs, white dwarfs, and cool dwarfs. We evaluate our method on LiDAR point clouds from the nuScenes and Waymo Open datasets to assess its resistance to coordinate-based adversarial attacks. Furthermore, we conduct experiments across various tasks, including classification, detection, and end-to-end driving, under both natural and adversarial conditions. Results demonstrate that TPC significantly improves robustness against attacks, yielding measurable gains in end-toedge driving under adversarial conditions. This paper introduces a geometric approach to verifying the correctness of algorithms during competitive programming contests. Ultimately, this approach has been implemented as a tool called "GeoPEC" (a Geo Principle Based Constructive Proof Checking System), which is available as open-source software.

Situational linear bandits represent a recently introduced model designed for personalized recommendation systems, particularly ones with high dimensionality that rely on deep neural networks for training. This model holds significant potential for application in distributed environments, such as the Internet of Things, where there is a desire to learn from multiple sources without accessing the data of others. In this work, we investigate the feasibility of learning a factual function from source agents to enable policy optimization in a target agent within a distributed situational linear bandit setting. We address this problem in an online context and propose learning algorithms that operate without direct access to target data. Specifically, we develop novel methods for the source agents and, for the first time, introduce protocols for context encoding and decoding suitable for this environment. Our theoretical findings indicate that the required number of source samples scales linearly with the dimensions of the factual function, reflecting the cost of learning these features from the source. Additionally, this count aligns with the square of the dimensionality of the source's situational space, accounting for the difficulty of inferring features from contextual information. Crucially, our results demonstrate that the necessity for source samples to learn the factual function depends on whether the target agent's policy is deterministic or stochastic. These outcomes are achieved through new technical contributions, including refined analysis of the Elf algorithm adapted to our specific context, as well as the development of innovative techniques for constructing events and establishing concentration inequalities. Ultimately, our approach requires no assumptions about the target agent's environment, requires no direct interaction with source data, and necessitates no communication between agents beyond encoding and decoding the target's contextual information. We conclude by outlining potential future research directions in this area.

We developed a global hydrodynamical model to investigate how dust growth influences hydrodynamic instabilities, specifically focusing on the vertical shear instability (VSI) in the outer regions of protoplanetary disks. Our linear analysis reveals that while gas cooling rates and dust mass loading primarily determine the VSI's growth rate, the instability's spatial extent is strongly dependent on dust properties, particularly the terminal velocity of dust grains. As dust cools the gas more effectively through optically thin thermal emission, the VSI's spatial scale increases; however, beyond a certain dust mass loading, the scale collapses because heavier grains settle faster due to higher terminal velocities. Similarly, increasing the average mass of dust grains produces analogous effects. Based on these findings, the optimal VSI growth occurs when the dust mass fraction is approximately $10^{-2}$ and the mean grain mass is around $10^{-6}$ g, corresponding to a scale of roughly 10 meters at 30 AU. Despite these constraints, the VSI remains viable across a wide range of external disk parameters, provided dust is present. Our study highlights that dust evolution plays a critical role in hydrodynamic instabilities, an effect that could be significant for turbulence generation in planetary atmospheres and the outer layers of stellar remnants like brown dwarfs and white dwarfs. Recent years have seen significant theoretical progress in deep neural networks (DNNs) for image and video recognition tasks. These models, however, are characterized by an enormous number of parameters, which, while delivering high accuracy, create substantial storage demands and limit practical deployment. This paper introduces a technique for compressing energy-efficient deep LSTM networks without compromising recognition performance. We propose a hybrid approach combining structural modifications and low-rank tensor decompositions. Specifically, we introduce five optimized layers: two fully connected layers converted into weight matrices, one input gate and one output gate transformed into low-order tensors, and two hidden layers decomposed into low-order tensors. Additionally, we designed a hardware architecture tailored to this compressed LSTM structure. To validate the efficacy of our method, we applied it to video surveillance for anomaly detection. Our results demonstrate that the proposed compressed LSTM achieves a 91.07% accuracy rate in identifying screaming anomalies, surpassing previous deep CNN and LSTM models. Furthermore, both the compression ratio and the improved accuracy are enabled by the hardware architecture optimized for the specific structure of our compressed LSTM. The significant increase in the compression ratio is directly attributable to the low-order tensor decomposition of the weight matrices. Ultimately, this work presents a high compression ratio and energy-efficient solution suitable for deploying deep LLMs on resource-constrained IoT devices. Regarding the low-order tensor decomposition, an alternative method known as Hierarchical Tucker (HTK) decomposition exists, which typically yields a higher compression ratio than the CP decomposition used in this study. Hypothesis testing serves as a fundamental method for evaluating scientific claims, with p-values and Bayes factors representing the two primary statistical approaches. While the integration of Bayes factors with replication constitutes a standard framework for the scientific method, its practical application has been limited by the labor-intensive nature of traditional workflows. This paper re-examines the principles of Bayes factors and replication to develop more efficient strategies for their computation. These optimized workflows enable the deeply repeated use of Bayes factors within a Bayesian analysis, a technique that has historically been advocated as a more rigorous alternative to the repeatedly applied p-values commonly found in data dredging or fishing expeditions. Although such extensive Bayesian analyses are computationally demanding, the resulting posterior distribution of Bayes factors offers a superior metric for assessing the strength of evidence compared to the distribution of Cp-values (the complement of p-values). Furthermore, the study revisits the debate between subjective and objective Bayesianism, demonstrating how an empirical distribution of Bayes factors can facilitate the determination of hyperpriors for Bayes factors in a fully objective Bayesian framework. The research concludes by applying these workflow strategies to a real-world scenario involving the search for new physics beyond the standard model at the Large Hadron Collider. Key terms include: Bayes factor, hypothesis testing, new physics, Large Hadron Collider, and objective Bayesianism.

Discourse indicators are linguistic elements that establish and maintain connections between sentences, playing a vital role in ensuring textual coherence. Although recent advances in natural language processing have attempted to identify these indicators using unsupervised, weakly supervised, and supervised methods, the resulting lists are often incomplete and include many false positives that fail to function as indicated in specific textual contexts. This research proposes an automated, context-aware approach for detecting and extracting discourse indicators from texts. Furthermore, the study presents a method for verifying the correctness of these indicators through a semi-supervised, iterative process applied to both simple and complex indicators. By integrating extraction and validation, we created an open-access corpus of over one million English texts labeled with complex discourse indicators, termed DiComp. Additionally, we developed a corpus of scientific texts labeled with meta-cognitive indicators, named DiMeta. Together, DiComp and DiMeta form a comprehensive corpus covering both simple and complex discourse indicators in English. We also introduced a suite of linguistic analysis tools based on these corpora called DiscSense, which utilizes various natural language processing techniques and manual evaluation to examine the properties of these indicators. Our findings reveal that current handcrafted rules for identifying complex indicators in English are insufficient and generate numerous false positives. We also observed that complex indicators are distributed non-uniformly across different academic disciplines, a pattern that aligns with human judgments regarding their appropriateness. Finally, we introduced a context-aware metric for evaluating unsupervised methods for discourse induction, which outperforms existing metrics in literature. To encourage further investigation into the gaps between simple and complex discourse indicators, we released the source code for DiscSense and the associated corpora at https://github.com/abhinav-rath/discsense.

This work introduces several tools for analyzing discourse indicators in English, an area that has seen limited automated exploration compared to other linguistic features. We argue that effective automation requires a multi-faceted set of tools, a concept we illustrate through our DiscSense framework. While some of these techniques may appear applicable to other languages, linguistic variations—such as the fact that our method for complex indicators relies on a corpus of paired texts—could necessitate adjustments for other linguistic environments.

Measurement of the local magnetic field is essential for numerous applications, including the operation of atomic interferometers and magnetometers, as well as the investigation of fundamental physics. In this study, we introduce a novel method to detect local magnetic fields with an atomic interferometer by leveraging the Meissner effect of a superconductor to modify the atomic wavefunction. Using this technique, we detect local field variations as small as $2.0 \pm 0.2$ nT per turn with a linear resolution of $0.5 \pm 0.1$ nT per turn and a resolution of $0.14$ nT over an integration time of $100$ s. This approach represents the first detection of local magnetic field changes via atomic interference through a material-based mechanism. The linear resolution is determined by the maximum current carrying capacity of the superconductor, whereas the ultimate resolution is influenced by the atomic acceleration sensor's sensitivity and the scale factor of the measurement system. Consequently, improving the linear and ultimate resolutions requires enhancing the critical current and acceleration sensitivity, respectively. This method offers a straightforward technique for calibrating the scale factor of local magnetic field sensors, such as those used in magnetometers and magnetically levitated gyroscopes. Furthermore, it provides an effective means to verify the sensitivity of other sensors designed for detecting minute field changes, including fluxgate magnetometers, optically pumped magnetometers, and SQUIDs. We anticipate that this method will find utility in various contexts, particularly in fundamental physics research involving magnetically levitated sensors and atomic sensors, as well as in quality control for other magnetic field sensors.
